Lewis-Clark Valley · Idaho–Washington

Project Rimrock The Living Machine

Idaho grew out of its mountains — timber down the rivers, power out of the rivers, towns where the rivers meet. On a canyon rim above the confluence of the Snake and Clearwater, a place is being planned that will tell that story the way it deserves to be told: working. Everything here will run in the open. The water will work. The railroad will haul. The mill will saw. The fire hall will answer. Nothing will be a picture of work — it will be work, and you will be inside it.

That’s the Idaho idea.

Walk the districts The story first
01

The Story

The path to modern

Rimrock’s districts walk a guest along the path this valley actually took — the rivers and the drives that floated an empire of white pine to Lewiston; the dam that turned a mountain river into light, and the hatchery that answered for the fish; the railroad, the mine, the mill — the industries that built the towns.

And the path does not end in a museum: it arrives at the modern — power protected by devices invented in a basement thirty miles away and manufactured in Lewiston today. The valley still invents.

From the mountains, to now.

The name is the land’s own

Farmers on this rim called their precinct Rim Rock, named for the basalt rim their farms sat on. The land told us where Rimrock has always been.

02

The Districts

Six districts · one machine

District 03

Caribel

A steam-powered sawmill designed so you follow one log from pond to boards — into the mill pond, up the carriage, through the saw, and out as lumber. The mill will not demonstrate sawing. It will saw.

District 04

The Rail Yard

Steam, the turntable, and a working railroad designed to haul real freight through the park. The yard is not a backdrop — it is how things here will get moved, on a schedule, under steam.

District 05

The Mine

The assay office, the headframe, the mountain’s other harvest. What the forests gave on the surface, the rock gave from below — and the towns were built on both.

01

The Hub

A railroad station crossed with a machine hall — the heart of the place, with two doors, where every district’s work will cross every other’s.

02

Firelands

A working two-bay fire hall, the drill ground, and the lookout tower — built to keep the valley’s oldest bargain: watch the high ground, answer the call.

06

Hotel Rimrock & Rimrock Springs

A railroad hotel grown out of the rim rock itself, and the waterworks under one roof — headrace, reservoir, the pumphouse, and The Works: the treatment plant in glass, built to work in the open for everyone to see and learn from.

03

The Living Machine

Everything connected

Everything is connected, everything has a reason, everything has a form and a function — and it is beautiful, because machinery is beautiful.

Water stored, dropped, worked, and returned. Steam on a schedule, whistles on the hour. A park built to run like the valley runs: in the open.

Rimrock is being planned as a living machine all the way through — its working systems will not be hidden behind the scenery. They will be the scenery, and they will teach while they run.

Water

The rule

The Land

Canyon-rim country

The Lewis-Clark Valley, Idaho–Washington. Canyon-rim country above the confluence of the Snake and Clearwater — basalt above, rivers below, and a working valley in between.

Being planned by Silverqueen Development Group — neighbors, building for neighbors.

“Neighbor helping Neighbor is important.”
